To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) The first-order Taylor method is a poor approximation for the second-order method, 2) The second-order method can prune 40-50\% of the weights in an optimally trained network with minimal loss in performance, 3) The second-order Taylor method is still an expensive approximation of the brute-force method, 4) There is a straightforward way to serially prune neurons from an optimally trained model with minimal loss in generalization performance.
\begin{itemize} \item The quality of pruning decisions is strongly dependent on the method used to make those decisions.

(1) pruning algorithms are not as effective as we think they are, and (2) the reason they aren’t effective is because we are not pruning the right neurons, and (3) there exists a straightforward method of pruning neurons in a way that preserves the learning representations of the pruned networks.

understanding the fundamental properties of neural network learning representations, and we hope that our findings will help inform future work on model compression.

What are the trade-offs we make when we choose to prune in a more computationally-efficient way? And what can we learn from pruning algorithms about the nature of learning representations in general?

the quality of the representation learned by a neural network depends primarily on the quality of the optimization method and secondarily on the size of the network.
the quality of the representation in the network does not depend on the number of neurons.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a novel algorithm for pruning neurons in a trained neural network that is more accurate than a first-order Taylor approximation and less expensive than a brute-force method.
we found the assumptions we make about how neural networks learn representations to be largely correct and the trade-offs in computational complexity to be justified.

we have found that pruning algorithms can be very useful tools for understanding the fundamentals of neural network representation learning, and that we should be more careful about how we use these tools.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the decision of which neurons to prune is more important than how to do the pruning itself.
pruning algorithms are an effective tool for analyzing how neural networks learn representations.

the quality of the representation learned by a neural network is not as sensitive to the size of the network as we might expect, and that we may be able to learn much more from pruning algorithms than we previously thought.
